sk-f1c972ce.stem: A footballer kicked on the outer side of the leg has a fracture of the neck of the fibula. When walking his toes scuff the ground, and sensation is lost on the dorsum of the foot. Which nerve is injured?
sk-f1c972ce.explanation: The common fibular nerve winds superficially around the outside of the fibular neck. When injured, the muscles of the anterior and lateral compartments are paralysed: foot drop, steppage gait and sensory loss on the dorsum of the foot and outer leg.

sk-11d29b23.stem: A 13-year-old boy who plays football has a painful, palpable swelling below the knee. Which structure is affected in Osgood–Schlatter disease?
sk-11d29b23.explanation: Osgood–Schlatter disease is an apophysitis caused by repeated traction of the patellar ligament on the tibial tuberosity apophysis during rapid growth. The force of the knee extensors is transmitted to the tibia through this prominence.

sk-31f5e5f7.stem: Which of the following is true of the lateral malleolus?
options: It is higher than the medial malleolus.
It does not articulate with the talus.
It is the distal end of the tibia.
The tibialis posterior tendon passes in the groove behind it.
It is lower and more posterior than the medial malleolus.
sk-31f5e5f7.explanation: The lateral malleolus is the lower end of the fibula, about 1 cm lower and further back than the medial malleolus. The fibularis longus and brevis tendons pass in the groove behind it. It articulates with the lateral surface of the talus and forms the outer limb of the ankle mortise.

sk-d87191b8.stem: Which tarsal bone has no muscle attachments?
sk-d87191b8.explanation: Most of the surface of the talus is covered with articular cartilage and no muscle attaches to it. Because its blood supply is limited and runs backwards, avascular necrosis of the body is common in neck fractures.

sk-8922c8d5.stem: Which tendon passes in the groove on the underside of the sustentaculum tali?
sk-8922c8d5.explanation: The shelf-like projection on the medial side of the calcaneus (sustentaculum tali) supports the talus. The FHL tendon passes in the groove for the flexor hallucis longus tendon on its underside; the FDL tendon runs near the medial edge of the shelf.

sk-966623d2.stem: Which is the main muscle attached to the tuberosity of the navicular?
sk-966623d2.explanation: The main tendon of tibialis posterior attaches to the navicular tuberosity, and its slips to the other tarsal and metatarsal bones. It is the strongest invertor of the foot and supports the medial longitudinal arch; its dysfunction is a common cause of acquired flat foot.

sk-e633c622.stem: Which tendon passes in the groove on the plantar surface of the cuboid?
sk-e633c622.explanation: The fibularis longus tendon crosses the sole in the plantar groove of the cuboid to attach to the medial cuneiform and base of the 1st metatarsal; it supports the transverse arch and everts the foot.

sk-e1c8c1c3.stem: A basketball player who rolled his ankle inwards has pain on the outer edge of the foot; X-ray shows an avulsion fracture at the base of the 5th metatarsal. Which muscle pulled off the bone fragment?
sk-e1c8c1c3.explanation: Fibularis brevis attaches to the tuberosity of the 5th metatarsal. In sudden inversion its contraction pulls off the tuberosity (avulsion fracture). A more distal fracture at the metaphyseal–diaphyseal junction (Jones fracture) is known for healing problems.

sk-afe30a76.stem: Which bone lies at the highest point of the medial longitudinal arch of the foot, in the position of the 'keystone'?
sk-afe30a76.explanation: The medial longitudinal arch is formed by the calcaneus, talus, navicular, three cuneiforms and medial three metatarsals. The head of the talus is the keystone at the top of the arch, supported below by the plantar calcaneonavicular (spring) ligament. The keystone of the lateral arch is the cuboid.

sk-8bab82f6.stem: Which nerve passes through the foramen ovale?
sk-8bab82f6.explanation: The mandibular nerve, accessory meningeal artery and lesser petrosal nerve pass through the foramen ovale in the greater wing of the sphenoid. Memory aid: 'Standing Room Only' – V1 leaves through the Superior orbital fissure, V2 through the foramen Rotundum, V3 through the foramen Ovale.
notes: It enters through the internal acoustic meatus.
It passes through the hypoglossal canal.
It passes through the foramen rotundum.
It passes through the superior orbital fissure.

sk-5f0b04cc.stem: Which structure passes through the foramen spinosum?
sk-5f0b04cc.explanation: The foramen spinosum lies posterolateral to the foramen ovale in the greater wing; the middle meningeal artery and the meningeal branch of the mandibular nerve (nervus spinosus) pass through it. The artery's anterior branch runs on the inner surface of the pterion and causes epidural haematoma in fractures.

sk-3c70aa92.stem: Which of the following does NOT pass through the jugular foramen?
sk-3c70aa92.explanation: Cranial nerves IX, X and XI, the sigmoid sinus and the inferior petrosal sinus pass through the jugular foramen. The hypoglossal nerve leaves the skull through the hypoglossal canal above the occipital condyle.

sk-cda51554.stem: Which structures pass through the optic canal?
options: Optic nerve and superior ophthalmic vein
Central retinal artery and trochlear nerve
sk-cda51554.explanation: The optic canal lies between the roots of the lesser wing of the sphenoid; the optic nerve passes through it with the ophthalmic artery below. The superior ophthalmic vein, III, IV, the branches of V1 and VI pass through the superior orbital fissure.

sk-711ff9cd.stem: Which nerve emerges from the stylomastoid foramen?
sk-711ff9cd.explanation: The facial nerve enters through the internal acoustic meatus, runs in the facial canal and emerges through the stylomastoid foramen between the styloid and mastoid processes; there it branches to the facial muscles before entering the parotid. In Bell's palsy, swelling in this narrow canal is blamed.
